Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi understood sadiq as describing the promise as truthful, a way of stressing its reliability. Ibn al-Qayyim noted that the winds, clouds, ships, stars and angels are all signs of the Creator's power, so the oath links them to the certainty of the promise. No commentator disputes the general sense of the verse.

God swears by the sky with its hubuk, meaning its tracks and well-made form. Most commentators understand hubuk as lines or traces, like those the wind leaves on sand or water, though others read it as the beauty and sound structure of the heavens. Ibn Abbas, Qatada, Mujahid and Ikrima explain it as fine creation and solid construction, al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr as adornment and the stars, while al-Dahhak, al-Kalbi and Muqatil take it as paths or traces. Ibn Zayd understands strength, and Abd Allah ibn Amr identifies it as the seventh heaven. The answer to the oath is, for most, that the unbelievers contradict one another about the Prophet and the Qur'an, calling him a sorcerer, a poet, a madman or a soothsayer. Scholars differ on what the pronoun in 'turned away from it' refers to: the Qur'an or the Prophet, so that whoever is turned away is turned away from it, or the contradictory speech itself, so that it misleads those already led astray; Mujahid reads the verb as being deprived of reason. The commentators support these meanings with lines of Arabic poetry, such as verses by Zuhayr and a rajaz, and they note several recitations of the word hubuk varying its vowels.

God swears by the heaven with its well-woven paths, and then states that you, the people of Mecca, are in a contradictory saying. The commentators agree that this divergence concerns what they said about the Qur'an and the Prophet ﷺ: some believed and some denied, as Qatada and Ibn Zayd report. They differ on how to define these opinions. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi understand it as a division among obedient and disobedient, believers and disbelievers, while Ibn Juraij sees polytheists contradicting one another in falsehood. Al-Kalbi, Muqatil and al-Zamakhshari relate that they called the Prophet a magician, a poet or a madman, and the Qur'an magic, poetry or fables of the ancients. Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi argue that this contradiction proves their claims false, since truth does not contradict itself. Al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd say the pronoun in 'is turned away from it' refers to the Qur'an or the Messenger, meaning that whoever is turned away from it is turned away. Others report that people turned away anyone wishing to embrace Islam by calling the message sorcery or soothsaying, a view attributed to Mujahid by al-Baghawi. Al-Zamakhshari considers that the pronoun may refer to the saying itself. Mujahid glosses 'ufika' as loss of reason, and Qutrub as deception. As for 'cursed are the fabricators', most read it as a curse on liars and doubters, and Ibn 'Abbas identifies them as the conspirators who divided among themselves the slanders against the Prophet to turn people from his religion.

God swears by the heaven of firm, well-made paths, which commentators understand either as the heaven itself in its beauty and evenness, as its stars, or as its orbits. He then states that the disbelievers hold contradictory views about the Qur'an and the Prophet ﷺ: some accept them and others reject them, calling him a sorcerer, a soothsayer, a poet or a madman. The commentators agree that the phrase 'turned away from it is whoever is turned away' means that whoever is led astray turns away from faith. They differ, however, on what the pronoun refers to. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi take it that whoever has gone astray is misled, al-Hasan and Qatada refer it to the Qur'an or the Messenger, and Ibn Zayd to the polytheists, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya allow that it refers to the contradictory statement itself, which is the cause of the turning away. Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Qayyim hold that this turning away is according to God's foreknowledge. On the meaning of the verb, Mujahid links it to loss of reason and Qutrub to deception, while al-Mawardi lists several related senses. Al-Sam'ani reports that the Quraysh sent people to warn travellers against the Prophet. Overall, the commentators read the passage as a rebuke of disbelief and of the confusion of those who deny the message.

The verse « Qutila al-kharrasun » says that those who guess and speculate about the truth, the fabricators of falsehood, are cursed and destroyed. Commentators differ on the sense of « qutila ». Ibn 'Abbas and most exegetes read it as « cursed », while Ibn al-Anbari holds that a curse is a kind of spiritual death, since one whom God curses is like a slain man, lost. Ibn 'Ashur and Ibn 'Uthaymin take it as a prayer for destruction, and al-Qurtubi reports that some read it as a wish that they be killed at the hands of the believers.

They also differ on who the « kharrasun » are. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Tabari and Mujahid name the doubters or soothsayers, al-Hasan those who deny resurrection, and al-Kalbi, with a second transmission from Ibn 'Abbas, the conspirators who divided among themselves plots against the Prophet. As for « kharṣ », al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi understand it as speaking without knowledge, al-Asamm as deliberate lying, and al-Tabari as mere conjecture.

The commentators agree that these people are immersed in ignorance and heedlessness, that they ask mockingly when the Day of Judgment will be, and that the divine answer tells them they will be tormented upon the Fire. On « yuftanun », al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Jalalayn take it as being tormented or burned, like gold tested in fire, while Ibn al-Qayyim links the ghamra to whatever veils the heart. The surah is Meccan by general consensus.

This verse describes those who deny the Last Day as immersed in ignorance and heedlessness, turned away from the truth and unable to reflect on what has come to them. The commentators explain the word "ghamra" as a veil of ignorance, doubt and error that covers the heart as water covers one who enters it, and "sahun" as being careless and forgetful of the matters of the Hereafter. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Ibn Zayd and as-Suddi largely agree on this meaning, and al-Tabari holds that these people persist in their misguidance.

The following verses report that they ask mockingly and in denial when the Day of Judgment will come. The answer is that on that day they will be tormented by the Fire. Commentators differ on the sense of the verb "yuftanun". Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrima, al-Hasan and al-Dahhak take it to mean being punished or burned, like gold tested in fire, while others read it as a sense of denial. Al-Tabari adopts the meaning of being burned.

The commentators agree that the verse is a warning that describes the state and fate of the deniers. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Uthaymin note that their question expresses disbelief and mockery rather than a genuine desire for knowledge.

This verse reports that the deniers ask, mockingly and with disbelief, when the Day of Judgment will come. The commentators explain that the question is not a sincere quest for knowledge but a way of denying and ridiculing. The answer follows in the next verse: on that day they will be exposed to the Fire and tormented in it. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy note that the word fitna here means torment and burning, compared to gold being tested in fire. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ikrima, al-Hasan and al-Zamakhshari hold this meaning of torment, while Mujahid also glosses it as burning and Ibn Abbas, in the words of ending, as denial. Al-Razi and Ibn Ashur stress the mocking tone of the question, which expects no real answer. Al-Tabari reports that grammarians of Basra took the word yawm as an adverb of time, while grammarians of Kufa held that it is indeclinable because it is attached to a clause, and Ibn Ashur and al-Qasimi treat it as an adverb of time governed by an implied verb. The commentators agree that the verse is a warning to those who deny the resurrection and ask for its arrival in derision.

This verse says that those who mockingly ask when the Day of Judgment will come will be tormented on that day, when they are presented before the Fire and burnt by it. The commentators agree that the word fitna here means punishment. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, following Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ikrima and al-Dahhak, explain that they are burnt as gold is tested in fire. Ibn Abbas also gives the word the sense of denial, so the torment is the consequence of their disbelief.

Al-Razi and al-Baghawi take the preposition 'ala' to mean they are placed over the Fire, or exposed to it. Al-Razi notes that the divine answer does not state the exact time, but rebukes their mockery. Ibn al-Qayyim sees several stages of fitna, from the trials of this world to the final punishment.

On grammar, al-Tabari records the views of the Basra and Kufa grammarians on the accusative of yawm: it is either a temporal accusative or an indeclinable form because of the clause that follows. Ibn 'Ashur and Abu Hayyan note that the nominative reading attributed to Ibn Abi 'Abla supports the second view. These differences do not change the overall meaning.

This verse addresses those who mocked the Day of Judgment and asked mockingly when it would come: they are told to taste their trial, that is, the punishment they had been demanding hastily in this world as a sign of their denial. Most commentators understand fitnatakum as torment or burning in the Fire, as al-Tabari, Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Zayd hold. Ibn Abbas understands it as their denial itself, meaning its consequence. Tasting is a metaphor for an intense experience of suffering. As for hadha, most treat it as the predicate of an implied subject, meaning this is what you were hastening, while Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan consider it an apposition to your trial. Ibn Kathir, al-Sa'di and Ibn 'Uthaymin take it as the Fire's punishment itself. Al-Razi explains that the phrase on the Fire means they are exposed to it, as gold is put to fire to be tested. Ibn Juzayy and Ibn 'Ashur note that yuftanun means being burned or tormented. Overall, the verse is a warning to the disbelievers, placed just before the description of the righteous who dwell in gardens and springs.

This passage describes the reward of the God-conscious in the Hereafter, after the mention of the punishment of the deniers: they will be in gardens and beside flowing springs. The commentators offer two readings of the phrase 'taking what their Lord has given them'. Al-Tabari and Ibn 'Abbas understand it as performing the obligations God prescribed, and read 'they were beforehand doers of good' as meaning before those obligations were imposed. Ibn Kathir, by contrast, takes 'taking' as a circumstance qualifying the gardens and springs, so the sense is that they receive with contentment the favours of God. Al-Zamakhshari reads the verb as accepting and being pleased, since all that is given them is good and agreeable. The exegetes agree that the goodness mentioned refers to their good deeds during life. For most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, the phrase 'they slept little of the night' means they devoted much of the night to prayer. They differ on the particle 'ma': al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir treat it as a relative or verbal particle, while some take it as a negation, meaning they hardly slept at all, a view transmitted from al-Dahhak and Muqatil. Anas ibn Malik, as cited by Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, explains it as prayer between sunset and the night prayer, whereas Mujahid and others say they stayed awake almost the whole night. Ibn 'Ashur notes that mentioning sleep portrays the soul's inclination to rest which these believers overcome. As for seeking forgiveness at dawn, many take it as prayer at that hour, others as asking for forgiveness in words. The verse adds that a portion of their wealth belongs to the beggar and the deprived. Ibn 'Abbas and others hold this to be a charity distinct from zakat, while Qatada and Ibn Sirin identify it with zakat. All agree that the beggar is one who asks out of need, and that the deprived is the modest person who refrains from asking and is thought well-off, alongside many other definitions recorded by al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi.

This verse describes the reward of the God-conscious in the Hereafter: they will be in gardens and among springs, taking gladly what their Lord has given them. Commentators differ on the meaning of 'taking'. Al-Tabari and Ibn Abbas, in one of his transmissions, understand it as performing the obligations God imposed in this world, while most exegetes, including Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Razi, take it to mean the blessings God gives them in Paradise, which they accept with contentment. Ibn Kathir and al-Razi consider this second reading more consistent with the structure of the verse. As for 'they were beautiful-doers before that', most commentators explain it as their good conduct in this life, and the verses that follow describe its signs: little sleep at night, seeking forgiveness at dawn, and giving a share of their wealth to the beggar and the deprived. Al-Tabari and Ibn Abbas connect the phrase to the time before the obligations were prescribed, whereas Ibn Kathir understands it as referring to deeds performed before entering Paradise. Ibn Abbas, Ibn Sirin and Qatada identify the rightful share of the needy as the obligatory zakat, while others, including Ibn Abbas in another report and Ibn al-Jawzi, see it as voluntary charity beyond zakat. The term 'the deprived' receives several definitions: the person who refrains from asking, the one who has no share in the spoils, or the one whose property was destroyed. Ibn Atiyya considers these as examples of one meaning rather than competing views. Grammarians also differ on the particle 'ma' in 'little of the night they slept': some take it as a superfluous particle, others as a negation or a verbal noun.

The verse describes the righteous who dwell in gardens and springs, receiving with approval what their Lord has given them, because they were doers of good before. On the phrase 'they used to sleep little of the night', the commentators explain that their sleep was brief and that they spent most of the night in prayer. Al-Tabari reports several early authorities: Ibn Abbas and Qatada said that they hardly ever passed a night without praying; Anas ibn Malik and Abu al-Aliya said they prayed between maghrib and isha; Muhammad ibn Ali said they did not sleep until they had prayed the night prayer; al-Hasan al-Basri held that they prolonged prayer until dawn. On the particle 'ma', al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy take it as a verbal (masdar) sense, meaning that their sleep was little; al-Zamakhshari, Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan treat it as an emphatic addition, while some grammarians read it as a negation, a view most exegetes consider weak. On 'they seek forgiveness at dawn', Dahhak and Mujahid take it to mean prayer, al-Hasan takes it as asking forgiveness, and Ibn Kathir notes that many link it to supplication offered with prayer. On 'a due right in their wealth for the beggar and the deprived', Ibn Abbas and Ibn Kathir understand a portion beyond obligatory zakat, whereas Qatada and Ibn Sirin identify it with zakat itself. Opinions on the deprived (mahrum) vary: one who has no share in the spoils, one whose property does not grow, one who is modest and does not ask, or one struck by a disaster to his harvest or herd.

The verse describes righteous believers who sleep little at night, spending most of it in prayer, and who ask their Lord for forgiveness at the hours before dawn. The commentators differ on the word "ma" in "they used to sleep but little of the night". Ibn Abbas, Qatada, Mujahid and al-Hasan read it as a sense of duration or a relative particle, which al-Tabari prefers: they slept little and spent most of the night standing in prayer. Anas ibn Malik and Muhammad ibn Ali add that they prayed between sunset and the night prayer. Al-Dahhak reads "ma" as a negation and stops after "little", so the sense becomes that they were few among people. As for "they seek forgiveness at the dawns", al-Hasan takes it as an actual request for forgiveness, while Mujahid, Ibn Umar and others take it as prayer. Ibn Kathir notes that many exegetes relate that Jacob postponed his request for forgiveness to the time of dawn. On the right in their wealth, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Sirin and Qatada identify it either with the obligatory zakat or with other gifts such as kinship ties and hospitality; Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi argue that since the surah is Meccan, it cannot refer to zakat, which was prescribed at Medina. On the "deprived", opinions differ: one who refrains from asking out of modesty, one whose livelihood has failed, or one with no share in the spoils. Ibn Atiyya considers these as examples of one single meaning, that of the person afflicted by deprivation.

The verse describes the righteous who will be in Paradise: they slept little at night, spending most of it in prayer, sought forgiveness at dawn, and set aside in their wealth a due portion for the beggar who asks and for the destitute who holds back from asking. The commentators differ on the nature of this due. Ibn Abbas, Ibn Sirin and Qatada take it to be the obligatory zakat, whereas al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy, noting that the surah was revealed in Mecca before zakat was legislated in Medina, understand it as voluntary charity beyond zakat, a view Ibn Atiyya also favours. On the meaning of al-Mahrum, opinions vary: Ibn Abbas and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab say it is the impoverished man who has no share in the community's provisions, al-Hasan and Ibn al-Hanafiyya say the one who has no share of the spoils of war, Qatada and al-Zuhri the modest poor man who does not ask, Zayd ibn Aslam the one whose harvest or livestock was destroyed, and Abu Qilaba the man whose wealth was swept away by a flood. Several scholars, including al-Razi and Ibn Atiyya, see these as examples of a single category: someone deprived of livelihood for whatever reason. Al-Sha'rawi notes that the verse does not say the due is fixed, and Ibn Sa'di adds that the verse covers both obligatory and recommended giving.

The commentators explain that the verse means there are clear signs and lessons on the earth of God's power and greatness, for those of firm certainty who benefit from reflecting on them. Qatada said that whoever travels the earth sees great lessons and signs. Al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and al-Zamakhshari list mountains, seas, rivers, trees and fruits, the variety of minerals and soils, and the way the earth is spread out like a carpet with paths between its regions. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Uthaymin stress that this variety is itself a sign, and that only the believer benefits from it. Al-Razi links the verse to the preceding promise, holding that these signs confirm the resurrection. Ibn 'Ashur sees in the regrowth of plants after they have dried a proof of revival after death. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Qayyim note that the word 'earth' covers its many regions. The scholars agree on the general sense and differ mainly on which examples to cite and on how the verse connects to its context.

The commentators explain that the verse "And in yourselves. Will you not then see?" calls the reader to reflect on the human being himself as a sign of his Creator. They differ on the details of these signs. Ibn al-Zubayr and Mujahid take them to be the passage of waste, since a person eats and drinks by one opening and expels by two, while Qatada and Ibn Zayd see the proportioning of the joints and limbs and the creation of man from dust before he spreads out as human beings. As-Suddi relates them to life, death, and what enters and leaves the body with food, and al-Hasan to old age after youth and weakness after strength. Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir mention the stages of formation from drop to clot to lump of flesh, and the variety of tongues, forms, colours and natures. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Juzayy stress the senses, reason, speech and the articulation of the limbs. Ibn Kathir considers all these readings acceptable, while at-Tabari chooses the sense that these signs show the oneness of the Creator, since none but Him can create such a being.

As for "And in the sky is your provision", Mujahid, Ad-Dahhak and Ibn Jubayr understand rain and snow, by which the earth brings forth its produce, while al-Hasan says provision is written in heaven and God withholds it from whom He wills because of sins. For "and what you are promised", Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi refer it to Paradise and Hell, Mujahid to good and evil, and Ibn Sirin to the Hour. They agree that the verse affirms the resurrection and the recompense.

The commentators explain that the words "And in the sky is your provision, and what you are promised" mean that the causes of your sustenance and the decrees concerning you come from above. Most, including Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak and Ibn Kathir, understand the provision to be the rain and snow by which the earth brings forth its produce and creatures live, rain being called "sky" because it descends from it. Al-Hasan reports that the provision is in the clouds, but people are deprived of it because of their sins. As for "what you are promised", some say it is Paradise and Hell, which lie above the heavens; others say good and evil, the Hour, or reward and punishment. Al-Tabari prefers the general sense, since God excluded no part of the promise or threat. Ibn Kathir notes that the meaning covers both spiritual and worldly provision. Al-Razi understands that provisions are measured out and recorded in the sky. On the oath "By the Lord of the heaven and the earth, it is indeed true, just as you speak", most exegetes take the object of the oath to be the promise and warning, the Quran, or the signs already mentioned. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr read "mithlu" in the nominative as an adjective of "haqq", while the others read it in the accusative; the comparison with human speech, however, conveys to all the sense of a certainty beyond doubt. The commentators agree that "sky" here means whatever is high, and that from there come provision and recompense.

God swears by His lordship over the heavens and the earth that what has been promised is a certain truth, as certain as your own speech. The commentators agree on the core meaning: the verse affirms the reality of sustenance, reward and resurrection, and the comparison with human speech is meant to show that no one should doubt it. They differ on what the pronoun "it" refers back to. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir link it to the signs and provision mentioned earlier, while al-Razi, al-Shawkani and others link it to what is promised, to punishment and reward, or to the Quran. Regarding the provision "in the sky", Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr understand it as rain, the cause of all sustenance, while al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin extend it to the reward and to the Hour. On grammar, most readers pronounce "mithla" in the accusative as a qualifier of an implied verbal noun, while Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr read it in the nominative as an adjective of "haqq"; al-Zamakhshari and others treat "ma" as an emphatic particle. Al-Hasan al-Basri reports that the Prophet said: "May God fight against people to whom their Lord swore by Himself and who did not believe." Commentators such as Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Kathir note that the comparison grounds certainty in an obvious, perceptible reality.

This passage recounts the story of Abraham's guests, the angels who came to bring him news of a son and to inform him of the destruction of Lot's people. The commentators present it as a consolation for the Prophet ﷺ and a warning to his people in light of the fate of nations that rejected their messengers. On the meaning of « the honoured », Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take it to mean that they are honoured with God, as the angels are described as honoured servants, while Mujahid, al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi hold that Abraham honoured them by serving them himself and hastening their meal. Al-Mawardi lists both senses without choosing between them. Opinions on their number range from three to twelve, and most name Gabriel and Michael among them. On the greeting, al-Tabari and Ibn Atiyya explain that the accusative « salaman » expresses a greeting by action, while the nominative in Abraham's reply signals permanence; Ibn Kathir considers the reply the better form. The Kufan reading « silm » is also noted. The commentators agree that Abraham did not recognise them, but differ on why: Ibn Abbas says he did not know them, Abu al-Aliya that their greeting was unfamiliar in that land, and al-Razi that they entered without asking permission. Abraham quietly went to his family to bring a roasted fatted calf, and when they did not eat he felt fear, which the angels calmed by announcing a knowledgeable son. Most identify him as Isaac, while Mujahid names Ishmael. His wife marvelled at bearing a child at her age, and the angels replied that this was the decree of the Wise, the All-Knowing Lord.

The verse describes the angels visiting Abraham in the guise of guests. They entered and greeted him with "salaman", and he replied with a fuller greeting, "salamun", then said they were people he did not know. The commentators stress that generosity toward guests is evident in the story: Abraham hurried to prepare a meal, bringing a fattened calf roasted, and withdrew quietly to his household so that the guests would not feel obliged to refuse. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi note that the description "honoured" may mean the guests are honoured by God, as in the verse about the angels as honoured servants, or that Abraham honoured them by serving them himself with his wife. As for his unease, Ibn 'Abbas explains that he did not recognise them, Abu al-'Aliya that he disliked their greeting in that land and time, and others that they entered without asking permission. Al-Razi holds that he found their appearance strange, neither that of men nor of the angels he knew. The readings differ between "salam" and "silm", and some scholars judge the nominal form of the reply more complete because it expresses permanence. The son announced is, according to the majority, Isaac, while Mujahid alone names Ishmael.

The verse describes how Abraham slipped away quietly to his household and returned with a fat roasted calf for his guests. The commentators read this as an act of honour: he hurried to offer hospitality without the guests noticing, and chose the best of his property, which according to Qatada was mostly cattle, a view repeated by al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn al-Qayyim explain that discretion is part of the host's good manners, so that the guest is not embarrassed or prevented from being served. Al-Razi stresses the speed implied by the connective particle, and Ibn Kathir describes the courtesies of the scene at length. On the verb raagha, Abu 'Ubayd reports that it is used only for a furtive departure, while al-Farra' says it implies concealing both going and coming back. Ibn Kathir and al-Jalalayn explain that the calf was roasted, and Abu Hayyan adds that it was prepared at once. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan observe that the question "will you not eat?" is a gentle invitation rather than a command. The verse contains no explicit legal ruling, but Ibn Kathir notes that Ahmad and other scholars derived from related texts the duty of hospitality towards a guest.

This passage tells how angels in the form of guests came to Abraham, who returned their greeting with a better one. He then quietly went to his family and brought a fat roasted calf, placed it before them and gently invited them: "Will you not eat?" The commentators agree that this offer was part of his generous hospitality: the food is set close to the guests, and the invitation is made as a polite offer rather than a command. Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn Kathir draw from it the rules of hospitality, and Ibn Uthaymin cites the hadith urging honour toward guests. As for their refusal to eat, most explain that angels do not eat. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan report instead that eating was a sign of safety among the Arabs, so Abraham feared their intent. Some also cite a report that the price of the meal is to mention God's name at the start and praise Him at the end. On the promised boy, the majority, including Ibn Jarir and Ibn Kathir, identify him as Isaac, while Mujahid says Ishmael; Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi reject this in light of the verse in as-Saffat. Most explain the word sarra as a cry, Qatada as a moan, and others as a group of women. On the act of striking the face, some say it was a slap, while Mujahid and as-Suddi say she struck her forehead in astonishment. The phrase "an old barren woman" is taken as a question: how can I bear a child, being old and barren?

The verse describes how the angels who came to Abraham in the form of guests did not eat the roasted calf he had brought them, and he felt fear inside himself, since a guest who does not eat his host's food is suspected of harmful intent. They reassured him that they were messengers of God and gave him the good news of a knowledgeable boy. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Atiyya agree that this son was Isaac, born to Sarah, although Mujahid, reported by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, said it was Ishmael; al-Tabari rejected this because the glad tidings were given to Sarah, not Hagar. On the meaning of 'alim, al-Tabari explains it as knowledgeable once he grows up, al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy stress that knowledge is the highest of the qualities announced, and al-Hasan al-Basri takes it to mean a prophet. Commentators hold that natural fear when its causes appear does not harm faith. The general sense is that a guest who refuses food arouses suspicion, and the good news was sent to dispel that fear.

This verse describes the reaction of Abraham's wife, Sarah, when she hears the angels' good news of a son. She comes forward crying out loudly, strikes her face in astonishment, and asks how she could bear a child at her age and being barren. The commentators agree on the general meaning: a mixture of shock and joy at news she finds impossible because of her old age and infertility. On the word sarra, most explain it as a cry or shriek, though al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy also link it to a wail, and Qatada and Ikrima describe it as a moan. Al-Qurtubi notes that some understood it as a crowd of women gathering. On the gesture of striking her face, Ibn Abbas takes it as a slap, while Mujahid, al-Sudi, Sufyan and Ibn Sabit describe a hand placed on the forehead in wonder, which al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi also report as a common gesture of women amazed at something. Al-Tabari and al-Mawardi give both readings. The son is named differently: most identify him as Isaac, while Mujahid says Ishmael. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Ashur support Isaac by noting that the promise concerned Sarah, not Hagar, who was Ishmael's mother. On the phrase 'an aged barren woman', the majority take it as a woman who never bore a child, with an implied question: how can I bear, or can an old barren woman bear? Ibn al-Qayyim sees in her brief words a model of modesty, while Ibn Kathir and Ibn Uthaymin report the angels' reply that this is the word of God, who is able to do all things.

This passage tells how the angels, having given Abraham the good news of a learned boy, also gave the news to his wife. She came forward crying out in astonishment and said that she was an old barren woman. The angels replied that this was what her Lord had said, so she should not be surprised, for He is the All-Wise and the All-Knowing. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, understand the promised son to be Isaac, and note that the promise came when both were already advanced in age. Mujahid, reported by al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi, held that the boy was Ishmael, a view Ibn 'Atiyya considered mistaken. Ibn 'Uthaymin distinguishes the 'learned boy' who is Isaac from the 'forbearing boy' who is Ishmael. The commentators differ over the cry: Ibn 'Abbas took it as a shout, Qatada as a moan, and others as an exclamation of wonder. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan explain that the angels speak of God's word, while Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn 'Ashur observe that mentioning wisdom before knowledge suits a birth that goes against the usual order. Overall, the commentators conclude that what seems impossible by human means comes to pass by the power and wisdom of God.

Abraham, having realised that his guests are messengers sent by God, asks them what their business is and why they have come. The commentators agree that the word khatb refers to a grave matter and a serious affair: Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi note that it is mostly used for hardships, while al-Razi explains that it signals the greatness of the matter and of those who are sent with it. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi explain that the question sought to learn the purpose of their mission. They reply that they were sent to a people of sinners, the people of Lot, to destroy them with stones of clay. Most exegetes, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, understand the clay as baked clay like brick. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Juzayy mention other views, such as that the stones were marked and not of this world, and Ibn Abbas and Mujahid add that each stone bore the name of its target. As for the survivors, the commentators agree that they were Lot and his two daughters, and Ibn Kathir specifies that Lot's wife was not saved. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi draw from this verse the conclusion that faith and Islam are one and the same, whereas Ibn Kathir considers that reading weak. The remaining sign is, according to Ibn Kathir, a foul-smelling body of water, and according to Ibn Jurayj a large stone, serving as a warning to those who fear painful punishment.

The commentators explain that when Abraham asked the angels about their mission, they replied that they had been sent to a criminal people, meaning, according to most exegetes, the people of Lot, who were guilty of disbelief and of the sin of sodomy. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi state that they were sent to destroy them with stones of clay, and al-Qurtubi says this clay was baked like brick until it became as hard as stone, while others hold that it was hardened by the sun over the ages. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir explain that the word musawwama means marked, each stone bearing the name of the person it was to destroy, and al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Ashur add that the stones were distinguished from the stones of this world. Ibn Abbas and al-Baghawi take the wasteful to mean the polytheists, since associating partners with God is the gravest of sins. The commentators agree that only Lot's household was saved, though they differ on the exact number, thirteen according to Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Tha'alibi, while Ibn Kathir and al-Razi note that Lot's wife was lost. On the difference between faith and submission, al-Zamakhshari, al-Qurtubi and al-Razi hold that every believer is a Muslim, whereas Ibn Kathir considers this inference weak. Ibn al-Qayyim observes that the sign left by this destruction instructs only one who fears the punishment of the Hereafter, and Ibn Ashur sees in the passage a warning to those who go astray.

The commentators explain that after the angels gave Abraham the good news of a son, they told him they had been sent to the criminal people of Lot to rain down stones of baked clay, sijjil according to many, hardened as stone is. Nearly all agree that 'musawwama' means marked, yet they differ on the mark: Ibn 'Abbas and al-Tabari describe white spots on a black stone or the reverse, al-Sam'ani and al-Qurtubi describe streaks of black and white or black and red, and others say each stone bore the name of its victim or resembled a seal. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi note that the clay is mentioned to distinguish these stones from hail, and Ibn 'Atiyya holds that they were not stones of this world. On those who were saved, all identify Lot and his household, but they differ on the number: Lot and his two daughters according to some, thirteen people according to others. Ibn Kathir notes that Lot's wife was excluded from the rescued. The phrase 'and We left in it a sign' is read in several ways: al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take it as a lesson and warning, al-Qurtubi and al-Shawkani as the stones or the ruined town, and Ibn 'Atiyya as black, foul water. Some have used the pairing of 'believers' and 'Muslims' in this passage to argue that the two terms are identical; Ibn Kathir replies that the overlap is specific to this situation, while Ibn al-Qayyim finds a subtler meaning tied to Lot's household. Ibn 'Ashur adds that hurling the stones is a metaphor and that their origin is volcanic material.

This verse describes the stones of baked clay that God sent down on the people of Lot, marked and kept with your Lord for those who transgressed. Scholars agree that "musawwama" means marked. Ibn 'Abbas described the stones as striped, either black and white or black and red, as Al-Qurtubi reports, and Al-Sam'ani, Al-Baghawi and Al-Zamakhshari relate that each stone bore the name of the person it was meant to strike. On the phrase "of clay", Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that the clay was fired like brick, while others say it hardened under the sun over time.

Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir identify the "musrifun" as those who overstep God's limits, and Ibn 'Abbas, Muqatil and Al-Baghawi take them to be polytheists. The following verse concerns the believers who were brought out of the city. Al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi say they were Lot and his two daughters, while Al-Tha'alibi and Ibn Kathir include his household except his wife; Al-Tha'alibi also reports the number as thirteen. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya take this passage to show that faith and Islam are one and the same, whereas Ibn Kathir considers that argument weak, since every believer is a Muslim but not every Muslim is a believer. Finally, Ibn al-Qayyim notes that the sign left for "those who fear the painful punishment" benefits only those who believe in the Hereafter, and Al-Tabari and Al-Qurtubi differ on whether the sign is the ruined city, the stones, or a foul black water.

This verse says that God brought out of the town of Lot's people those who were believers before the punishment fell on them. The commentators agree that the reference is to Lot and the members of his household who believed in him, and that the pronoun "in it" refers to the town even though it had not been mentioned, since it was well known. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that these believers were Lot and his two daughters, while Ibn Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, as cited by Ibn Kathir and al-Suyuti, speak of a group of thirteen people. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qasimi note that Lot's wife, although part of the household outwardly, was not among those saved. On the relation between faith and submission, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi hold that the two terms refer to the same reality, whereas Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Ashur, al-Shawkani and Ibn 'Uthaymin distinguish inner faith from outward submission, so that every believer is a Muslim but not every Muslim is a believer. Al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy emphasise that God's favour preserved the righteous among the wrongdoers.

This verse says that God brought out from the town of Lot's people those who had faith, and that He found in it only one house of Muslims, the house of Lot. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi, understand the house to be Lot and his two daughters, judging from the context. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that the believers are described as both believers and Muslims because every believer is a Muslim. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya, however, note that faith is inward assent of the heart and Islam outward submission, so the two terms differ. Al-Sam'ani and al-Nasafi hold that faith and Islam are one and the same, while Ibn Kathir considers this argument weak, the coincidence of the two terms here being due to the particular situation. Qatada reports that had there been more believers in the town, God would have saved them too. Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn 'Ashur see in Lot's wife someone who outwardly professed Islam without being a believer, and Ibn 'Uthaymin counts her among those destroyed. As for the rest of the verse, most commentators take the remaining sign left for those who fear the painful punishment to be the ruins, the stones, or the foul black water, according to the reports they cite.

This verse states that God left in the towns of Lot's people a lasting sign and lesson of the punishment He sent upon them, one from which those who fear the painful punishment can benefit. The commentators agree that the town is Sodom, and that the pronoun "in it" refers back to it even though it is not named. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report that its ruin remained visible. They also agree that the only household of believers found there was that of Lot, namely Lot and his two daughters, although Sa'id ibn Jubayr, as cited by Ibn Kathir, counts thirteen people in all.

The commentators differ on what the sign was. Ibn Jurayj says it was a great quantity of stones piled up, while Ibn Kathir, Abu Hayyan and al-Razi speak of black, foul-smelling water or a stinking lake, and al-Razi adds that the stones were scattered between Syria and the Hijaz. Al-Zamakhshari reports both views without choosing between them. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the town was left in ruins, and that this desolation is itself the sign.

Al-Razi and al-Nasafi note that the lesson benefits those who fear punishment, not hardened hearts. Ibn al-Qayyim links this to belief in the Resurrection, without which such signs bring no lesson. Ibn 'Uthaymin adds that the sign may be both physical and moral.

The commentators explain that the verse refers to the story of Moses, whom God sent to Pharaoh with a clear authority, and that this mission is a sign and a lesson. They agree that the clear authority (sultan mubin) means a manifest proof, which some identify as the staff and the hand, and others as the miracles in general. For the phrase he turned away with his rukn, most take it to mean that Pharaoh turned away from faith, but they differ on the meaning of rukn. Ibn Zayd, Mujahid, Ibn Abbas and Qatada understand it as his troops, his people or his strength, al-Akhfash as his side, and Muqatil as his deviation from the truth and his obstinacy. Al-Mawardi adds that it could refer to his wealth. As for the words sorcerer or madman, most read or as a choice or a division of accusations, while Abu Ubayda, al-Farra and al-Mu'arrij read it as meaning and, since both charges were made together; Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan consider this reading weak and unnecessary here. The commentators connect the passage with the accounts of punishment before it, such as 'Ad, Thamud and the people of Noah, presented as warnings for those who fear the painful punishment. Some relate the opening wa-fi Musa to the earlier verse about signs on the earth, others to the statement that God left a sign there.

This verse describes how Pharaoh turned away from Moses after he had brought a clear proof, relying on his power and his army, and then called him a sorcerer or a madman. The commentators agree on the core meaning: Pharaoh turned his back on faith. They differ on the word rukn, meaning support or pillar. Ibn Zayd, Mujahid and Ibn Kathir take it to mean his troops and companions, while Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada understand it as his strength and power. Al-Akhfash reads it as his side, and Muqatil as his deviation from truth through stubborn disbelief. Al-Mawardi adds that it could mean his wealth, and al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya see the phrase as a figure for complete aversion.

Regarding the accusation of sorcery or madness, most commentators take the "or" as a presentation of alternatives, or a deliberate ambiguity, since Pharaoh could not decide between them. Abu 'Ubayda, al-Mu'arrij and al-Farra' argue that "or" means "and", because he said both, citing a line by Jarir; Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan find this unconvincing. Al-Sam'ani notes the contradiction, since sorcery requires full reason. Al-Razi explains that the sorcerer seeks out the jinn by choice, whereas the madman is approached against his will.

The exegetes conclude that God seized Pharaoh and his armies and cast them into the sea, and that he was deserving of blame for his disbelief and arrogance.

This verse tells us that God seized Pharaoh and his armies, threw them into the sea, and they drowned, while Pharaoh was deserving of blame for what he had done. The commentators agree that "nabadhnahum" means to cast away, and that "al-yamm" is the sea. The clause "wa huwa mulim" is a circumstance showing that Pharaoh had committed what deserves blame. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi, al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that this blame refers to disbelief, obstinacy, claiming lordship, and denying the messengers, a reading also given by al-Jalalayn. Al-Tabari reports that Qatada took it as blame for being ungrateful for God's favours. As for the "rukn" on which Pharaoh turned, al-Mawardi lists several meanings: his troops, his strength, his side, or his wealth, and al-Tabari favours the sense of soldiers and power. The text then turns to 'Ad, whose "barren wind" is, according to Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada, one that fertilises no trees and brings neither rain nor good. Its direction is disputed: Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab holds it was the south wind, while al-Mawardi and Ibn Kathir cite the tradition about the east wind and the west wind. On the meaning of "ramim", opinions range from dried straw to dust, ash, and decayed bones.

This verse states that the destruction of the people of 'Ad is a sign and a lesson, for God sent against them the barren wind, a wind with no good or blessing in it, which neither fertilised trees, nor raised clouds, nor brought rain, but was purely a wind of destruction. The commentators explain that it reduced to ruin whatever it passed over, whether people, livestock or property, leaving it like crumbled, dried-out debris. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi agree on the general meaning of 'barren' as a wind that does not impregnate or bring forth growth. They differ, however, on its direction. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, al-Harith ibn 'Abd al-Rahman and one report from Ibn 'Abbas call it the south wind, while Muqatil, al-Suyuti and al-Mahalli take it to be the west wind, dabur, citing the hadith that the east wind was the means of victory and 'Ad was destroyed by the dabur. Mujahid and another report from Ibn 'Abbas identify it with the east wind, sabā, while 'Ali, in a report Ibn 'Atiyya considers unsound, names the nakba, an intermediate wind. As for 'rameem', Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid take it to mean what is perished and decayed, Qatada what is dry plant trampled underfoot, al-Suddi and Abu al-Aliya powdered dust, and Qutrub ash.

The commentators read this verse as part of the account of the peoples who were destroyed: it mentions the people of 'Ad, upon whom God sent a barren wind, meaning one without any good in it, which neither fertilised trees nor brought rain, but served only to destroy. They all agree that this wind reduced to dust whatever it passed over, like something dry and crushed. The meaning of 'rameem' is discussed: Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid take it to mean what is perished and decayed, Qatada what dry plants trodden underfoot become, al-Suddi and Abu al-'Aliya crushed earth, Qutrub ashes, and al-Zajjaj dry, crumbled leaves. As for the wind itself, opinions differ: Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab says it was the south wind, while Muqatil, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi say it was the west wind, relying on the hadith 'I was helped by the east wind, and 'Ad was destroyed by the west wind'. Ibn 'Abbas describes it as a wind between two others, and the reports attributed to 'Ali are considered unreliable by Ibn 'Atiyya because they contradict that hadith. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir note that the generality of the phrase is restricted to what God willed to destroy, as Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan also state. Al-Razi adds that the wind acted under a divine command, as though it truly targeted 'Ad and their homes.

The commentators explain that this verse mentions another sign in the people of Thamud, when their prophet Salih told them to enjoy themselves until the end of their terms. Some take this as the three days after the slaughter of the she-camel, as stated elsewhere: enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days. They then became arrogant and disobeyed the command of their Lord, and the thunderbolt, meaning the annihilating punishment, seized them while they were looking on. Most exegetes understand al-sa'iqa as a destroying punishment. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir hold that al-hin refers to the appointed time of death, while Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Farra' and al-Qurtubi take it to mean the three days following the camel's slaughter. Al-Razi finds the general sense of each person's appointed term more likely, since the particle fa indicates that the rebellion came after the order to enjoy life. On recitation, most read al-sa'iqa, while al-Kisa'i, and according to some reports 'Umar, read al-sa'qa, the cry itself. Several commentators note that the people could neither rise nor defend themselves, and that the punishment was witnessed openly in daylight. According to al-Baghawi and others, their waiting for punishment over three days was harder than the punishment itself.

The commentators explain that this verse, within the series of stories about peoples who rejected their prophets, tells how the Thamud were told to enjoy their lives in their homes for a set time, either until the end of their lives or for three days after they hamstrung the she-camel. They became arrogant and disobeyed the command of their Lord, and the thunderbolt seized them while they were looking on. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy agree that al-sa'iqa is the destroying punishment, that 'ataw means arrogance and refusal to submit, and that they saw their destruction with their own eyes because it came in broad daylight. Al-Tabari and Mujahid report that the Thamud waited for the punishment for three days, during which its signs appeared, so that waiting was harder for them still. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi stress that the event was sudden. The readings differ: most read al-sa'iqa, while al-Kisa'i and 'Umar ibn al-Khattab read al-sa'qa, which Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya take to mean a single cry. On the meaning of 'hatta hin', Ibn 'Atiyya prefers the time of death, and notes that the particle fa shows the rebellion came after that command. Al-Razi and Abu Hayyan observe that the verb takes 'an rather than 'ala, which highlights refusal. Finally, all note that they could neither rise nor defend themselves.

This verse says that Pharaoh's people could neither rise nor flee when the punishment struck them, and that no one defended them. The commentators agree on this general meaning but differ on the word qiyam. Al-Tabari, Qatada, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Baghawi take it to mean rising from their fallen state, while Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Razi, al-Nasafi and others take it to mean being able to repel the punishment, an Arabic idiom for being unable to cope with something. Al-Razi notes that saying they were not able is stronger than saying they could not do it. Regarding muntasirin, most explain it as those who defend or protect themselves, and al-Zamakhshari relates it to escaping the punishment. On the reading of Qawma Nuh, al-Tabari reports that Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim read it in the accusative, while Abu 'Amr, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it in the genitive, linking it to the preceding passage on Moses and 'Ad, and al-Tabari considers both readings valid. The commentators draw no legal rulings from this passage. They treat it mainly as a lesson on the helplessness of those who reject the messengers before God's decree.

This verse states that the people of Noah, who were destroyed before 'Ad, Thamud and the people of Pharaoh, were a people who defied God and departed from His command. Commentators see it as the final element of a sequence of accounts about nations that rejected their prophets. The main point of debate concerns grammar and recitation: Abu 'Amr, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read «qawmi» in the genitive, linking it to the preceding «wa fi Thamud», so that the sense is «and there is a sign in the people of Noah», while most readers use the accusative «qawma», meaning «and We destroyed the people of Noah», or link it to a preceding pronoun, or treat it as governed by an implied verb such as «remember». Al-Tabari considers both readings valid, and Ibn 'Ashur notes that the accusative is the more common. All agree that «min qabl» means that this people was destroyed before the others. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Jaza'iri stress that Noah preached for a very long time while few believed, and that their drowning is a lesson. Al-Razi also notes how the following verse about the building of the sky supports the argument of divine power. The word «fasiqin» is understood by most as departing from obedience, while al-Nasafi renders it as disbelievers.

God states in this verse that He built the heaven with power and strength. Most commentators explain the word "bi-aydin" as meaning force, as reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada, and al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi follow this reading. Ibn 'Ashur explains that "al-ayd" means strength, while Ibn 'Uthaymin notes that it is not the plural of "hand" but a noun meaning strength. On the phrase "wa inna la-musi'un", the views differ. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, al-Qutaybi and al-Tabari take it to mean power or wealth and abundance, al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd understand it as providing abundant sustenance through rain, Mujahid as a power able to create a heaven like it, and Ibn Zayd and Ibn 'Ashur as enlarging the heaven. Al-Razi finds the sense of vast space or the ability to recreate closest to the meaning. The commentators agree that this verse, placed after the mention of the earth and of pairs, recalls the greatness of creation as evidence for resurrection and prepares the call to flee to God and abandon idolatry. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir see in the pairing of creatures a sign of the unity of the Creator. Some extend the "pairs" to all opposites such as night and day or faith and disbelief, while others limit them to male and female, and al-Tabari prefers the first sense. In short, the verse glorifies God's power in creating the heaven, the earth and pairs, and the differences over the meaning of expansion and of pairs do not change the general message that calls people to recognize the greatness of the Creator and His oneness.

This verse states that God spread out the earth as a bed and prepared it as a cradle on which creatures can settle, and that the praise in "how excellent are the ones who spread it" refers to God himself. Commentators agree that the verb "spread" means to lay out and level, and that the "spreaders" are those who make a place fit for dwelling. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur explain that the earth was made suitable for dwelling, planting, resting and walking. Ibn 'Abbas said that God arranged for his servants what suits them. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Zamakhshari see in the spreading a sign of divine wisdom, since a humped earth would hurt the walker and the one lying down. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Biqa'i developed the idea of preparation for human use. One point of difference concerns extent: al-Sam'ani reports from al-Naqqash that the earth spans a five-hundred-year journey, and Ibn al-Jawzi cites Muqatil for the same measure, while also citing Qatada, who gives twenty thousand farsakhs; Ibn al-Jawzi finds the first measure far-fetched but does not settle between them. Al-Sa'di stresses the variety of its benefits, and al-Sha'rawi links the verb to the earth's changeability.

The commentators explain that God created two kinds of every thing, meaning two opposite categories or two distinct species, so that people may remember His power and recognize that the Creator of these pairs is one and alone deserving of worship. They offer several examples. Mujahid lists disbelief and faith, happiness and misery, guidance and error, night and day, heaven and earth, while others name male and female, and al-Hasan names the sun and moon, sea and land, death and life. Al-Tabari prefers Mujahid's view because it shows the power that brings opposites into being, whereas fire and snow each do only one thing.

Ibn Zayd, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi focus on male and female within each kind of living thing, and Ibn Kathir extends the pairs to light and darkness, life and death, paradise and hell. Al-Razi explains that every genus divides into two species, which proves that the Creator is one. Al-Alusi and al-Qasimi add that the remembrance may concern the difference between what is possible and what is impossible, or the resurrection.

All agree that the purpose is reflection, so that people realise the Creator of pairs has no partner, as al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir state. Ibn 'Ashur reads the word "perhaps" as an invitation to think. Al-Sha'rawi notes that modern science has found duality in the atom and in electricity, while Ibn 'Uthaymin observes that some human beings were created without a father or a mother.

This verse calls people to flee from God's punishment towards His mercy, that is, to return to Him through repentance, faith and obedience. The Prophet ﷺ is presented as a clear warner sent by God. The commentators explain the verb 'flee' in closely related ways. Ibn Abbas, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand it as escaping God's torment towards His reward through faith and obedience, while Sahl ibn Abd Allah says it means fleeing from all that is other than God towards God, and al-Junayd that it means fleeing from Satan, who calls to falsehood, towards God, who protects. Al-Mawardi, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya take it more as a return to obedience and repentance from sin. All the commentators link the passage to the affirmation of God's oneness that immediately follows, namely the prohibition of associating another god with Him. Al-Zamakhshari explains the repetition of the warning formula as showing that faith does not benefit without works, nor works without faith. Ibn al-Qayyim distinguishes two senses: fleeing to God belongs to the oneness of worship, and fleeing from God to God belongs to the oneness of lordship and divine decree. Al-Sha'rawi widens the flight to anything that opposes divine law, such as desires and Satan. Ibn Ashur sees a metaphor for abandoning polytheism, since the address is to the idolaters.

This verse tells people not to set up any other god alongside God, and states that the Prophet is a clear warner sent to them from Him. The commentators read it as the continuation of the earlier call to flee to God: fleeing means returning to Him through faith, obedience and repentance, and then the prohibition of associating partners names the very thing from which one most needs to flee. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi explain that fleeing to God means turning back to Him by repentance and by giving up disobedience, while Ibn 'Abbas says it means fleeing His punishment towards His reward through obedience.

The repetition of the warning has drawn particular attention. Al-Zamakhshari sees in it the point that faith benefits only together with good deeds and deeds only together with faith. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn 'Ashur take it as an emphasis that strengthens the admonition, and al-Nasafi holds that prolonging the threat is more eloquent. Al-Razi links the mention of God to monotheism: affirming that God exists and denying that there are several gods.

Most commentators agree on the general sense, which is a break with everything opposed to God. Al-Qurtubi cites Sufi readings that describe this flight as a passage from ignorance to knowledge, from disbelief to gratitude, or from self to one's Lord. Ibn Sa'di understands the verse as the basis of fleeing to God, which means abandoning idols and tombs to devote oneself to Him alone. The scholars differ mainly on the details of the expression and the purpose of the repetition, and not on its central meaning.

This verse shows that Quraysh were not the first to reject messengers: every people before them called their prophet a magician or a madman, and the earlier disbelievers acted as the present ones do. Commentators explain that "Kadhalika" points back to this rejection, or simply means "it is so." Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi read the question "did they charge one another with this?" as a rebuke, and God then answers that rebellion, not a shared plan, united them. Al-Zamakhshari says they could not have conspired because they did not live in the same age, and Ibn Kathir adds that their hearts resembled one another. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that the people of Lot never called their prophet a magician, so the word "or" divides the groups. Al-Razi answers the objection that not every prophet was rejected by saying that one who confirms the law of an earlier prophet is not a messenger. Al-Alusi raises the same difficulty and offers several answers, the most likely being that the wording refers to the majority rather than to all. Ibn 'Ashur sees the "min" in "min rasul" as a sign of generality. Al-Shinqiti and Ibn Sa'di stress the similarity of hearts. All the commentators agree that the verse consoles the Prophet ﷺ by reminding him that other messengers suffered the same.

This verse says that the earlier peoples who rejected their messengers each called them a sorcerer or a madman. It then asks, in a tone of reproach and surprise, whether they had charged one another with this saying so that they all agreed on it. The commentators answer that they had not made any such arrangement. Al-Tabari, citing Qatada, says the first generation charged the last with denial, but then concludes that these people were simply rebels who exceeded their limits. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Nasafi, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud agree that the word 'bal' rejects the idea of mutual instruction and affirms that arrogance and transgression drove each one to speak this way, which explains why their words resemble each other. Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di follow this reading and cite the verse 'their hearts have become alike'. Al-Razi reads the question as expressing wonder at a unanimity that looks deliberate, and explains that what united them was prosperity, which made them forget God and turn against the messengers, like a king who lets his people live in comfort and then calls them back to his court and sees them turn away. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi note that 'tughyan' means going beyond bounds and rising up on earth in opposition to God. On the lines that follow, most commentators hold that the command to turn away from these people was abrogated by the verse 'remind, for the reminder benefits the believers', while Ibn 'Atiyya and others read the turning away as giving up excessive zeal and exhausting effort, not abandoning the preaching itself. Ibn 'Ashur stresses that the similarity of their statements comes from a shared disposition of the hearts, not from a coordinated instruction.

In this verse God tells His Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, to turn away from the polytheists who reject him and leave them alone, for he bears no blame since he has conveyed the message and fulfilled his duty. The commentators explain that the verb tawalla means to turn away and abandon. Al-Tabari, citing Mujahid, reads it this way, while al-Jazairi adds that this withdrawal lasts until God's decree comes upon them. Most agree that the Prophet was not negligent and that the blame falls on those who refuse, as al-Razi points out. Several report that when the verse was revealed the Companions were grieved, believing revelation had stopped and punishment was near, and that the following verse, "Remind, for reminder benefits the believers," reassured them, according to al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi. On abrogation, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy consider the verse abrogated, some by the verse of reminder and others by the verse of the sword. Ibn 'Ashur reads the turning away as ceasing to insist in debate, while the call to remind remains in force. Al-Qasimi rejects the reading that the Prophet should abandon preaching altogether. Most commentators agree the message had been delivered fully and the Prophet was not at fault.

In this verse God tells His Prophet ﷺ to turn away from the stubborn polytheists to whom he has repeatedly issued the call, for he is not to be blamed once he has delivered the message. He is then ordered to continue admonishing and reminding, because the reminder benefits the believers. Most commentators understand the reminder as admonition through the Quran, while Mujahid takes it as general exhortation and al-Zajjaj and al-Kalbi as reminding people of God's days, His punishment and His mercy. The exegetes report that the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ were distressed when the command to turn away was revealed, thinking revelation had ended and punishment was near, and their hearts were relieved when the verse of reminder came down. Most exegetes hold that the verse of turning away was abrogated by the verse of the sword, while others limit the abrogation to the matter of conciliation. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur explain that turning away does not stop the reminding, which remains useful: it strengthens the believers and establishes proof against those who oppose. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Uthaymin stress that only believers truly benefit from the reminder, and that one who is unmoved by it has a deficiency in his faith.

This verse states that God created jinn and humankind only to worship Him, and the commentators read the word worship in several ways. Ibn Abbas, whose view al-Tabari adopts, explains that it means that they acknowledge His lordship, willingly or unwillingly. Ali ibn Abi Talib and al-Zajjaj take it as meaning that God commands them to worship Him, while Mujahid understands it as "that they may know Me," a reading that Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi consider excellent, since creation leads to knowledge of God's existence and oneness. Zayd ibn Aslam links it to the destiny written for each creature, the fortunate being made for worship and the wretched for disobedience. Al-Qurtubi, al-Nasafi and others report that some scholars restrict the verse to believers from both groups, citing Ibn Abbas's reading "from among the believers." Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Juzayy stress worship freely chosen, and Ibn al-Qayyim underlines that God has no need of His creatures.

Regarding the next phrase, "I do not want any provision from them, nor do I want them to feed Me," the commentators agree that God is free of all need. Ibn Abbas and Abu al-Jawza' explain that He does not want them to provide for themselves, while others take it as an affirmation that God alone is the Provider. Ibn Kathir cites the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud about God as the Provider, the Possessor of strength, and several scholars note the differing readings of the word al-matin.

The commentators explain that this verse affirms that God has no need of the provision or food of His creatures: He is the absolutely Rich, who provides without being provided for. As for the phrase 'I do not want from them any provision', al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most exegetes take it to mean that God does not ask them to provide for His servants or for themselves, while Ibn 'Abbas and Abu al-Jawza' understood it as meaning they do not feed themselves. Attributing the feeding to God himself is explained by al-Baghawi and others: creatures are God's dependants, and whoever feeds the dependants of someone has fed that person, a point supported by hadiths quoted by Ibn Kathir. Al-Zamakhshari contrasts this with masters who use their slaves to earn a living, which God does not do. Al-Razi argues that the negation extends even to serving a meal, and that the order of the terms moves from the general to the particular. The readings 'al-Razzaq' and 'al-matin', with their grammatical variants, are also recorded. Ibn 'Uthaymin and Ibn Sa'di stress that the purpose of creation is worship and that God gains nothing from it, a point echoed by al-Sha'rawi.

The commentators explain that God alone is the Provider of all His creatures, the One who ensures their sustenance, and that He possesses a strong and unshakeable power. They agree that the verse gives the reason for what precedes it: God does not seek provision or food from people, for He is the Self-Sufficient. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most scholars take 'strength' to mean perfect power, and 'al-matin' to mean the very firm. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Ata' explain 'al-matin' as 'the mighty'. The majority reading is 'al-matinu' in the nominative, describing God; Yahya ibn Wathhab and al-A'mash read it in the genitive, describing 'strength'. Al-Farra' justifies the masculine by the image of a tightly twisted rope, while al-Tabari prefers the nominative because the readers agree on it.

Regarding 'a portion like the portion of their fellows', the commentators agree that the reference is to the disbelievers of Mecca. The word 'dhanub', originally a large bucket of water, here means a share or a portion, and Qatada explains it as a bucket of punishment. On 'let them not seek to hasten it', al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi hold that the punishment is deferred until the Day of Resurrection, whereas Abu Hayyan and al-Jaza'iri see it as a punishment that is certainly coming. As for 'the Day they are promised', most identify it with the Day of Resurrection, while some say it is the Day of Badr.

Al-Razi notes that the pairing of 'strength' with 'firmness' expresses a power that is stable and cannot be shaken.

The commentators explain that this verse warns the disbelievers of Mecca who wronged themselves by denying the Prophet ﷺ: they will receive a share of punishment like that of the nations before them, so they should not ask for it to be hastened. Most read the word dhanub as a portion or share, drawn from the image of a large bucket of water, as Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatada reported, while others take it to mean the punishment itself, a portion of torment or a rope-bucket full of it. Nearly all agree that "their companions" are the earlier nations who denied their messengers, such as the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud, and they place the verse within the consolation offered to the Prophet. They differ on the day mentioned in the next verse: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand it as the Day of Resurrection, while others report it to be the day of Badr, and Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Juzayy judged the first view stronger. As for the phrase "so let them not seek to hasten it", al-Tabari, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi read it as a prohibition on hastening a punishment that will surely arrive at its appointed time, whereas al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan detect irony. Ibn Kathir and al-Alusi stress the threatening character of the verse, and Ibn 'Uthaymin notes that the respite given to the wrongdoer is no escape from punishment.

The commentators explain that the verse "So woe to those who disbelieved, from their day which they are promised" means ruin and severe punishment for the disbelievers on the day they were promised the punishment to descend. They differ on which day is meant. Most exegetes, including Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi, Abu al-Su'ud, al-Shawkani and Ibn 'Ashur, understand it as the Day of Resurrection, and Ibn Juzayy prefers this because it fits the opening of the surah, while Ibn 'Abbas, Muqatil and others, reported by Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi, take it to be the day of Badr, which al-Alusi notes better fits the immediate context. All connect the word "woe" (wayl) with evil and distress, and some add that it names a valley in Hell. The preceding verses explain that the disbelievers will receive "a portion like the portion of their counterparts" from earlier nations, and that they should not seek the punishment hastily. Al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi recall that "dhanub", originally a large bucket of water, came to mean a share or portion. Read plainly, the verse is a stern warning to those who deny, pointing to a fixed day that will not be missed, whether that is the Last Day or Badr.
